title: Ranking Features with Binary and Multiclass Fisher Scores
description: Define fisher_score_binary and fisher_score_multiclass as ratios of between-class variance to within-class variance per feature, then sort and plot the 4 Iris feature scores.
source: draft: agy free model + edit: codex

steps.description: Define `fisher_score_binary(X, y)`: split `X` into `X0` and `X1`, and compute per-feature means `mu0, mu1` and sample variances `v0, v1`. Return the squared mean difference divided by the sum of variances plus the supplied stabilizing term.

Define `fisher_score_multiclass(X, y)` and compute the overall weighted mean `mu = np.average(means, axis=0, weights=counts)`. Accumulate weighted between-class squared differences `num += counts[i]*(means[i]-mu)**2` and within-class variances `den += counts[i]*Xc.var(axis=0, ddof=1)`. Return `num` divided by `den` plus the supplied stabilizing term.
Compare line 8 and lines 19-21: both formulas score every feature independently by dividing how far apart the class means are (`num`) by how spread out each class is internally (`den`).

steps.question: Why does the ordering expression reverse `np.argsort(F_multi)`, and which two Iris features rank highest in multiclass Fisher score?
steps.answer: `np.argsort` sorts indices from smallest to largest, so reversing them gives descending order. This places `petal length (cm)` (`F=15.2036`) and `petal width (cm)` (`F=14.1315`) at the top.

steps.description: Evaluate `F_multi = fisher_score_multiclass(X_tr, y_tr)`, print the features in descending `order`, and draw a bar chart of `F_multi[order]`.
